title: Session 10: Towards Inclusive Societies: Global Challenges and Perspectives
text:
NoteGuiding question



How can inclusive societies be developed in the context of global social, political, ecological and technological transformations?


The final session brings the perspectives of the seminar together and asks how inclusive and just societies can be shaped under conditions of global transformation, and where the limits lie.


Topics

Preconditions of inclusive societies
Empowerment and participation
Inclusive governance and political participation
Social resilience and cohesion
Sustainable development and social justice
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Possibilities and limits of international inclusion strategies



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Social Resilience
Empowerment
Inclusive Governance
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)





Social Resilience
Core idea. Social resilience describes the ability of individuals, communities and societies to cope with crises, adapt to change and, where necessary, transform. In the face of climate change, economic crises and pandemics, the concept has gained great importance.
Aim of the theory. To understand how social groups and institutions can deal with shocks and long-term change without losing participation and cohesion.
Key claims

Resilience includes coping capacities (dealing with immediate shocks), adaptive capacities (learning and adjusting) and transformative capacities (changing structures).
Resilience depends on resources, social networks, institutions and power relations.
Resilience is unequally distributed: marginalised groups often have fewer resources to cope.
Collective resilience can be strengthened through social cohesion, trust and functioning institutions.
Transformation means changing the conditions that produce vulnerability in the first place.

Key concepts: coping, adaptive and transformative capacities · vulnerability · social capital · cohesion · transformation
Criticism. Critics argue that the resilience concept can depoliticise inequality and shift responsibility to individuals and communities (“be resilient”) instead of changing structures.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. For social work, resilience is a familiar concept at the individual level. At the societal level, it raises the question of how institutions can protect marginalised groups in crises.
Key reading: Keck, M./Sakdapolrak, P. (2013): What Is Social Resilience? Lessons Learned and Ways Forward. Erdkunde 67 (1), 5–19.




Empowerment
Core idea. Empowerment refers to processes in which people and groups gain more control over their lives and the conditions that affect them. It has roots in social movements, community psychology and Paulo Freire’s pedagogy of the oppressed.
Aim of the theory. To strengthen the self-determination and collective agency of marginalised people instead of treating them as passive recipients of help.
Key claims

Empowerment works at several levels: individual, group/community and structural/political.
Paulo Freire describes education as a process of critical consciousness (conscientização) through which people recognise and change oppressive conditions.
Julian Rappaport understands empowerment as a process by which people gain mastery over their affairs.
Empowerment focuses on strengths and resources rather than deficits.
Professionals act as facilitators, not as experts who decide for others.

Key concepts: self-determination · critical consciousness · strengths perspective · collective agency · participation
Criticism. Critics warn that empowerment is often reduced to individual self-optimisation and used to justify withdrawal of state support. There is also a paradox: can one “empower” others from above?
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Empowerment is a key principle of social work. It links inclusion with participation and power: inclusion means not only being included, but being able to shape conditions.
Key reading: Freire, P. (1970): Pedagogy of the Oppressed. New York: Herder and Herder. · Rappaport, J. (1987): Terms of Empowerment/Exemplars of Prevention. American Journal of Community Psychology 15 (2), 121–148.




Inclusive Governance
Core idea. Inclusive governance means that decisions in politics and public institutions are made with the participation of those affected, especially marginalised groups. It concerns not only outcomes, but the processes of decision-making.
Aim of the theory. To make institutions more responsive, legitimate and just by broadening participation in decision-making.
Key claims

Participation can range from information and consultation to real co-decision and control.
Sherry Arnstein’s ladder of citizen participation distinguishes non-participation, tokenism and citizen power.
Inclusive governance requires accessible procedures, resources and the removal of barriers.
The principle “nothing about us without us” from the disability rights movement expresses this claim.
Inclusive governance links inclusion with democracy and representation.

Key concepts: participation · ladder of participation · tokenism · co-production · representation · accountability
Criticism. Participation processes are often criticised as symbolic. Those with more resources tend to participate more, which can reproduce inequality.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Inclusive governance calls on social work to enable participation of addressees, both in services and in local politics, and to avoid merely symbolic involvement.
Key reading: Arnstein, S. R. (1969): A Ladder of Citizen Participation. Journal of the American Institute of Planners 35 (4), 216–224. · Fung, A. (2006): Varieties of Participation in Complex Governance. Public Administration Review 66, 66–75.




Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Core idea. In 2015, the member states of the United Nations adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development with 17 goals and 169 targets. Unlike earlier development goals, the SDGs apply to all countries and link social, economic and ecological dimensions.
Aim of the theory. To provide a global framework for sustainable development that “leaves no one behind”.
Key claims

The SDGs include goals on poverty (SDG 1), education (SDG 4), gender equality (SDG 5), decent work (SDG 8) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).
The principle of leave no one behind places the most marginalised groups at the centre.
The goals are universal: they apply to the Global North as well as the Global South.
Social, economic and ecological sustainability are understood as interconnected.
Progress is monitored through indicators and national reviews.

Key concepts: 2030 Agenda · leave no one behind · universality · SDG 10 · indicators · sustainability
Criticism. Critics point to the large number of goals, their non-binding character and tensions between economic growth and ecological limits. UN progress reports show that many targets are off track.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The SDGs offer a common reference framework for inclusion policies. For social work, they provide arguments for linking local practice with global goals.
Key reading: United Nations (2015): Transforming Our World: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. A/RES/70/1. New York: United Nations.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 8: Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Discrimination and Social Exclusion
text:
NoteGuiding question



How can artificial intelligence and algorithmic decision-making reproduce or intensify social inequalities?


This session examines how artificial intelligence and algorithmic decision-making can reproduce existing inequalities and produce new forms of discrimination.


Topics

AI and social decision-making
Algorithmic bias and algorithmic discrimination
Automated decisions and institutional inequality
Surveillance, data protection and social control
Power and inequality in digital societies



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Algorithmic Bias
Algorithmic Discrimination (Safiya Umoja Noble)
Surveillance Studies (David Lyon)





Algorithmic Bias
Core idea. Algorithmic systems are often presented as neutral and objective. In practice, they can produce systematically unfair results for certain groups. Algorithmic bias describes such distortions, which arise from data, design decisions or the context of use.
Aim of the theory. To understand how and why automated systems discriminate and how such effects can be identified and reduced.
Key claims

Algorithms learn from historical data; if these data reflect discrimination, the system reproduces it.
Proxy variables such as postcode or name can stand in for protected characteristics such as ethnicity.
Feedback loops can reinforce bias, for example in predictive policing.
Well-known examples include risk assessment in criminal justice in the USA and the Dutch childcare benefits scandal, in which a risk model contributed to the wrongful targeting of families, many with a migration background.
Bias can arise at every stage: problem definition, data collection, model design and use.

Key concepts: training data · proxy variables · feedback loops · fairness · transparency · accountability
Criticism. There is no single definition of fairness; different fairness criteria can be mathematically incompatible. Technical fixes alone cannot solve problems rooted in social inequality.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Algorithmic systems are increasingly used in welfare administration, employment services and child protection. Social work must understand their risks and advocate for affected people.
Key reading: Barocas, S./Selbst, A. D. (2016): Big Data’s Disparate Impact. California Law Review 104, 671–732. · Eubanks, V. (2018): Automating Inequality. New York: St. Martin’s Press.




Algorithmic Discrimination · Safiya Umoja Noble
Core idea. In Algorithms of Oppression, Safiya Umoja Noble shows how search engines reproduce racist and sexist stereotypes, especially about Black women and girls. She argues that such results are not accidental errors, but a consequence of commercial interests and social power relations.
Aim of the theory. To show that digital technologies are not neutral and to analyse how they reinforce racism and sexism.
Key claims

Search results reflect and amplify dominant stereotypes.
The commercial logic of search engines, based on advertising, shapes what becomes visible.
Marginalised groups have little control over how they are represented online.
“Technological redlining” describes how digital systems reinforce existing social exclusions.
Public information should not be left solely to private, profit-oriented companies.

Key concepts: technological redlining · representation · search engines · commercial logic · intersectionality
Criticism. Some critics argue that the focus on individual examples makes it difficult to generalise. Search engines have also changed since the study, although the underlying problems remain topical.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The approach links digital technologies to racism and sexism. It sensitises students and practitioners to how online representations shape the image of marginalised groups.
Key reading: Noble, S. U. (2018): Algorithms of Oppression: How Search Engines Reinforce Racism. New York: NYU Press. · Benjamin, R. (2019): Race After Technology. Cambridge: Polity.




Surveillance Studies · David Lyon
Core idea. Surveillance is a central feature of modern societies. David Lyon understands it as the systematic collection and processing of personal data in order to influence or manage people. He emphasises that surveillance sorts people into categories with unequal consequences.
Aim of the theory. To analyse surveillance not only as a threat to privacy, but as a social practice that produces inequality.
Key claims

Surveillance is everyday and ubiquitous: in workplaces, consumption, migration control, social services and online platforms.
Surveillance works as social sorting: people are classified, and these classifications affect their life chances.
Marginalised groups, such as benefit recipients, migrants or racialised minorities, are often subject to more intensive surveillance.
Data collected for one purpose are increasingly used for others.
Shoshana Zuboff describes a “surveillance capitalism” in which personal data become a commodity.

Key concepts: social sorting · dataveillance · surveillance capitalism · privacy · categorisation · control
Criticism. Critics argue that the concept of surveillance is sometimes stretched too far and that the benefits of data use are underestimated. Distinguishing legitimate from illegitimate surveillance remains contested.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Social services collect large amounts of personal data. Surveillance studies raise the question of how help and control are connected and how addressees’ rights can be protected.
Key reading: Lyon, D. (Ed.) (2003): Surveillance as Social Sorting. London: Routledge. · Zuboff, S. (2019): The Age of Surveillance Capitalism. New York: PublicAffairs.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 6: Environmental Justice, Climate Change and Exclusion
text:
NoteGuiding question



How does climate change reinforce existing inequalities and create new forms of social exclusion?


This session explores the social dimensions of the ecological crisis: how environmental burdens and climate change reinforce inequality and hit disadvantaged groups hardest.


Topics

Climate change and social inequality
Environmental justice and climate justice
Environmental racism
Unequal distribution of ecological risks
Climate-related migration and displacement
Global responsibility and intergenerational justice



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Environmental Justice (Robert Bullard)
Climate Justice
Environmental Racism
Climate Migration





Environmental Justice · Robert Bullard
Core idea. Environmental burdens are not distributed randomly. Landfills, toxic waste sites and polluting industries are disproportionately located in poor neighbourhoods and communities of colour. Robert Bullard’s research in the USA helped found the environmental justice movement and its scholarly analysis.
Aim of the theory. To show that environmental problems are social problems and to demand equal protection and participation for all communities.
Key claims

Environmental risks follow existing lines of social inequality, especially race and class.
Disadvantaged communities have less political power to resist the siting of harmful facilities.
Environmental justice includes distributive justice (who bears burdens and benefits), procedural justice (who participates in decisions) and recognition (whose knowledge and needs count).
Protests in Warren County, North Carolina (1982) against a toxic waste landfill are seen as a starting point of the movement.
Environmental justice is now also applied globally, for example to waste exports and resource extraction.

Key concepts: distributive, procedural and recognition justice · environmental burdens · community participation · grassroots movement
Criticism. The concept was developed mainly in the US context and must be adapted to other societies. Measuring the causal link between discrimination and environmental burdens is methodologically demanding.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Environmental justice shows that exclusion also takes place through living conditions, health and space. For social work, environmental conditions in neighbourhoods are part of addressees’ life situations.
Key reading: Bullard, R. D. (1990): Dumping in Dixie: Race, Class, and Environmental Quality. Boulder: Westview Press. · Schlosberg, D. (2007): Defining Environmental Justice. Oxford: Oxford University Press.




Climate Justice
Core idea. Those who contributed least to climate change are often hit hardest by its consequences. Climate justice links climate change to questions of global and intergenerational justice and asks who bears responsibility and who bears the costs.
Aim of the theory. To frame climate change not only as an environmental or technical problem, but as a question of justice and human rights.
Key claims

Historical emissions come mainly from industrialised countries of the Global North.
Poorer countries and groups are more vulnerable and have fewer resources to adapt.
International climate policy recognises common but differentiated responsibilities.
Debates concern mitigation, adaptation, finance and loss and damage; a fund for loss and damage was agreed at COP27 in 2022.
Climate justice also includes intergenerational justice: future generations bear the consequences of today’s emissions.

Key concepts: historical responsibility · vulnerability · common but differentiated responsibilities · loss and damage · intergenerational justice
Criticism. There is controversy over how to allocate responsibility (by historical emissions, current emissions or per capita) and how to balance climate protection with development needs. Climate policy measures themselves can also burden poorer households.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Climate justice links global inequality to everyday life: energy poverty, heat, housing and health. It asks social work to consider ecological dimensions of social inequality.
Key reading: Roberts, J. T./Parks, B. C. (2007): A Climate of Injustice. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. · Shue, H. (2014): Climate Justice: Vulnerability and Protection. Oxford: Oxford University Press.




Environmental Racism
Core idea. Environmental racism refers to policies and practices that expose racialised groups disproportionately to environmental hazards, whether intended or not. The term was coined in the context of the US civil rights movement in the 1980s.
Aim of the theory. To name the racist dimension of environmental inequality and to link environmental struggles with anti-racist movements.
Key claims

Race is a strong predictor of exposure to environmental hazards, in some studies stronger than income.
The 1987 report Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States documented this pattern for hazardous waste sites.
Environmental racism works through decisions on land use, housing segregation and unequal enforcement of environmental laws.
It need not be intentional; structural and institutional mechanisms are sufficient.
Globally, the concept is applied to waste exports, extraction on indigenous land and the externalisation of pollution to the Global South.

Key concepts: environmental racism · racialised exposure · structural racism · segregation · racial capitalism
Criticism. Critics discuss how to separate the effects of race and class. Some scholars argue that the concept should be linked more closely to analyses of capitalism and the state.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept connects this session with Session 2 (coloniality) and with institutional racism. It shows that racism also affects health and living environments.
Key reading: United Church of Christ Commission for Racial Justice (1987): Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States. New York. · Pulido, L. (2017): Geographies of Race and Ethnicity II. Progress in Human Geography 41 (4), 524–533.




Climate Migration
Core idea. Climate change affects human mobility, for example through droughts, floods, sea-level rise and loss of livelihoods. Climate migration describes movements in which environmental and climatic factors play a significant role.
Aim of the theory. To understand the links between climate change and migration and the gaps in legal protection for those affected.
Key claims

Most climate-related mobility takes place within countries, not across borders.
Migration is usually multicausal: climate factors interact with poverty, conflict and governance.
People displaced by climate change are generally not refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention; there is a protection gap.
The poorest people may be “trapped” because they lack the resources to move.
World Bank projections suggest that tens of millions of people could become internal climate migrants by 2050 if no action is taken.

Key concepts: climate-related displacement · internal migration · multicausality · protection gap · trapped populations · planned relocation
Criticism. Terms such as “climate refugees” are criticised as legally imprecise and as feeding alarmist scenarios of mass migration. Numbers are difficult to estimate.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Climate migration links Sessions 5 and 6: environmental change becomes a new mechanism of exclusion, and legal status decides on protection.
Key reading: World Bank (2021): Groundswell Part 2: Acting on Internal Climate Migration. Washington, DC: World Bank.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 4: International Welfare State Models and Social Protection
text:
NoteGuiding question



How do different welfare state models promote or restrict social inclusion?


This session compares welfare state models and asks how political and institutional frameworks shape access to social rights, resources and participation.


Topics

Development and functions of the welfare state
International welfare state models
Social protection and poverty reduction
Universalism and selectivism
Social rights and access to benefits



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Welfare Regime Theory (Gøsta Esping-Andersen)
Social Protection
Universalism versus Selectivism





Welfare Regime Theory · Gøsta Esping-Andersen
Core idea. Welfare states differ not only in how much they spend, but in how they organise the relationship between state, market and family. Gøsta Esping-Andersen distinguishes three “worlds of welfare capitalism”, each with its own logic of inclusion and exclusion.
Aim of the theory. To compare welfare states systematically and to explain why they produce different patterns of inequality.
Key claims

Decommodification: the degree to which people can maintain a livelihood without depending on the market.
Stratification: welfare states do not only reduce inequality, they also create their own hierarchies.
The liberal regime (e.g. USA, UK) relies on the market and means-tested benefits.
The conservative-corporatist regime (e.g. Germany, France) links benefits to employment and status and supports the traditional family.
The social-democratic regime (e.g. Sweden, Denmark) offers universal, generous benefits and promotes equality.

Key concepts: decommodification · stratification · state–market–family · liberal, conservative and social-democratic regimes
Criticism. Feminist critics (e.g. Jane Lewis, Ann Orloff) argue that the typology ignores gender and care. Others identify additional regimes, for example a Mediterranean model, and question its usefulness for countries outside Western Europe.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The theory shows that access to social rights and the risk of exclusion depend on the welfare regime. It helps to compare how countries treat unemployed people, families or migrants.
Key reading: Esping-Andersen, G. (1990): The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism. Cambridge: Polity.




Social Protection
Core idea. Social protection comprises all public measures that protect people against poverty, vulnerability and social risks across the life course. In global social policy, it has become a key instrument for reducing poverty and promoting inclusion.
Aim of the theory. To secure a minimum of income and access to essential services for everyone and to protect against risks such as illness, old age, unemployment or disability.
Key claims

Social protection includes social insurance (based on contributions), social assistance (needs-based) and universal benefits.
The International Labour Organization (ILO) calls for national social protection floors that guarantee basic income security and essential health care for all.
Many people worldwide, especially in the Global South and in informal work, still lack effective social protection.
Approaches such as “transformative social protection” stress that social protection should not only provide relief, but also address power relations and discrimination.
Cash transfer programmes in the Global South are an important example.

Key concepts: social insurance · social assistance · universal benefits · social protection floor · transformative social protection · informal work
Criticism. Critics point out that social protection programmes are often underfunded, conditional and targeted in ways that exclude people. They may also stabilise rather than change unequal structures.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept makes visible that large parts of the world’s population lack basic protection. For social work, it raises questions of access, take-up and conditions of benefits.
Key reading: International Labour Organization: World Social Protection Report (latest edition). Geneva: ILO. · Devereux, S./Sabates-Wheeler, R. (2004): Transformative Social Protection. IDS Working Paper 232. Brighton: IDS.




Universalism versus Selectivism
Core idea. Should social benefits go to everyone or only to those in need? This question divides social policy. Universal benefits are granted to all members of a group; selective benefits are targeted, usually through means tests.
Aim of the theory. To compare the advantages and disadvantages of both principles for inclusion, efficiency and social cohesion.
Key claims

Universal benefits, such as child benefit for all families, avoid stigma and reach almost everyone entitled.
Selective benefits concentrate resources on the poor and appear more efficient at first sight.
Means tests can deter people from claiming benefits (non-take-up) and stigmatise recipients.
Richard Titmuss argued that universal services form the basis on which selective support can be provided without stigma.
Walter Korpi and Joakim Palme described a “paradox of redistribution”: systems targeted at the poor often reduce poverty less, because they enjoy less political support.

Key concepts: universal and selective benefits · means test · targeting · stigma · non-take-up · paradox of redistribution
Criticism. Universal systems are expensive and can benefit people who do not need support. Selective systems are cheaper but can create poverty traps and stigma. In practice, most welfare states combine both principles.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The choice between universalism and selectivism determines who is included and how. For social work, non-take-up and stigma are everyday problems in accessing benefits.
Key reading: Titmuss, R. M. (1968): Commitment to Welfare. London: Allen & Unwin. · Korpi, W./Palme, J. (1998): The Paradox of Redistribution and Strategies of Equality. American Sociological Review 63 (5), 661–687.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 2: Postcolonial and Decolonial Perspectives
text:
NoteGuiding question



To what extent do colonial power relations continue to shape contemporary forms of social inclusion and exclusion?


This session examines how colonial power relations still shape inequality, belonging and exclusion today, with a focus on the construction of difference and the global hierarchy of knowledge, cultures and societies.


Topics

Colonialism and its social consequences
Postcolonial relations of power and domination
Othering and the construction of the stranger
Eurocentrism and hierarchies of knowledge
Decolonisation and global justice



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Postcolonial Theory (Edward Said, Homi K. Bhabha)
Decolonial Theory (Aníbal Quijano, Walter Mignolo)
Coloniality of Power (Aníbal Quijano)





Postcolonial Theory · Edward Said, Homi K. Bhabha
Core idea. Colonialism did not end with formal independence. Its images, categories and forms of knowledge continue to shape how the world is seen and how difference is produced. Postcolonial theory analyses these continuities, above all in culture, language and representation.
Aim of the theory. To reveal how colonial knowledge constructed the “Other” and how these constructions still legitimise inequality and exclusion.
Key claims

Edward Said shows in Orientalism that Western scholarship, art and politics constructed “the Orient” as irrational, backward and static, and the West as its rational counterpart.
Such representations are not neutral: knowledge and power are closely linked, and representation served colonial rule.
Homi K. Bhabha emphasises ambivalence: colonial discourse is never complete or stable.
Concepts such as hybridity, mimicry and the third space describe how colonised subjects appropriate, imitate and subvert dominant culture.
Identities are not fixed essences, but are produced in relations of power.

Key concepts: Orientalism · othering · representation · knowledge and power · hybridity · mimicry · third space
Criticism. Critics argue that postcolonial theory focuses too much on texts and discourse and neglects material and economic inequality. Bhabha’s concepts are also seen as abstract and difficult to apply empirically.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The theory helps to recognise how images of “the Other” justify exclusion, for example in migration debates or development policy. For social work, it calls for reflection on one’s own categories and representations of addressees.
Key reading: Said, E. W. (1978): Orientalism. New York: Pantheon. · Bhabha, H. K. (1994): The Location of Culture. London: Routledge.




Decolonial Theory · Aníbal Quijano, Walter Mignolo
Core idea. Modernity and coloniality are two sides of the same coin. The decolonial approach, developed mainly by Latin American scholars, argues that European modernity was built on colonial domination, and that this domination continues in economic, political and epistemic forms.
Aim of the theory. To make visible the colonial foundations of modern knowledge and institutions and to open space for other ways of knowing and living.
Key claims

Modernity, which presents itself as progress and universality, has a “darker side”: coloniality.
Coloniality persists after the end of colonial administration, in hierarchies of race, labour, gender and knowledge.
Eurocentric knowledge claims universal validity and devalues other forms of knowledge.
Walter Mignolo calls for epistemic disobedience and delinking from Eurocentric frameworks.
The goal is a pluriverse: a world in which many worlds and forms of knowledge can coexist.

Key concepts: modernity/coloniality · coloniality of power and knowledge · Eurocentrism · epistemic disobedience · delinking · pluriversality
Criticism. Critics warn that the approach can construct “the West” and “the non-West” as homogeneous blocks and romanticise indigenous knowledge. It is also pointed out that decolonial theory is itself largely produced in Western universities.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The approach questions who defines what counts as valid knowledge, development and inclusion. For social work, which has largely Western roots, it raises the question of how far its concepts and methods are transferable to other contexts.
Key reading: Mignolo, W. D. (2011): The Darker Side of Western Modernity: Global Futures, Decolonial Options. Durham: Duke University Press. · Mignolo, W. D./Walsh, C. E. (2018): On Decoloniality. Durham: Duke University Press.




Coloniality of Power · Aníbal Quijano
Core idea. With the colonisation of the Americas, a new global power structure emerged. Its core is the classification of the world’s population according to the idea of “race”. Quijano calls this structure the coloniality of power. It outlasted colonialism and still organises social relations today.
Aim of the theory. To explain why racial hierarchies, global divisions of labour and Eurocentric knowledge remain closely intertwined.
Key claims

“Race” is a modern invention: a mental category that naturalised colonial domination.
Racial classification was linked to the global control of labour: unpaid or forced labour for colonised populations, wage labour mainly for Europeans.
Capitalism, racism and Eurocentrism developed together as one global pattern of power.
Eurocentrism is the epistemic side of this pattern: it presents European experience as universal.
Formal decolonisation did not abolish this pattern of power.

Key concepts: coloniality of power · race as classification · global division of labour · Eurocentrism · historical-structural heterogeneity
Criticism. The concept is criticised for its strong focus on the Americas and for treating “race” as the central axis, which may underestimate other forms of domination, such as gender, as María Lugones has argued.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept links current racism and exclusion, for example on labour markets or in migration regimes, to their historical origins. It shows why anti-discrimination work must address structures, not only prejudices.
Key reading: Quijano, A. (2000): Coloniality of Power, Eurocentrism, and Latin America. Nepantla: Views from South 1 (3), 533–580.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text: The boundaries of inclusion and exclusion are shifting. Four developments are particularly important: globalisation, migration, digitalisation and broader social transformation. Each of them creates new opportunities for participation and new forms of exclusion.

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Globalisation
Global markets connect societies more closely. Production, capital and information move across borders. At the same time, the gains are unevenly distributed. Some regions and groups benefit, while others lose jobs and security. National welfare states have less room to manoeuvre. Exclusion can thus have causes far beyond the local level, and local social work encounters its consequences.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Migration
Migration is a normal feature of modern societies. It raises the question of who belongs and under what conditions. Residence status, citizenship rules and asylum procedures create graded forms of membership, from full citizens to people with temporary protection or without papers. Debates on migration often serve to draw symbolic boundaries between “us” and “them”. At the same time, migrants and their descendants claim participation and change societies from within.

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Digitalisation
Digital technologies open new forms of access to information, education, services and political participation. They also create new divides. Research distinguishes several levels of the digital divide: access to devices and internet, skills to use them, and the benefits people can actually derive from them. As public services move online, those without access or skills risk being cut off. Algorithmic systems in recruitment, credit scoring or social administration can reproduce discrimination, often in ways that are difficult to see and to contest.

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Social transformation
Further developments reshape inclusion and exclusion: climate change and its unequal consequences, demographic ageing, changes in work and employment, growing inequality and political polarisation. Several crises overlap and reinforce each other. They put pressure on welfare systems and can increase competition for resources. In such situations, the willingness to include others may decline, and exclusionary rhetoric can gain support.

section: What this means for the seminar
text:
What this means for the seminar
These developments show why the topic remains relevant. Inclusion and exclusion are not settled questions. They are renegotiated under changing conditions.
For social work practice, this means keeping both levels in view: supporting people in concrete situations and analysing the broader transformations that shape their lives. The following parts of the seminar take up these challenges in an international comparison.

Which of the four developments affects the addressees of social work in your region most strongly? Give a concrete example.

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text: Inclusion is usually seen as the positive counterpart to exclusion. This view is too simple. Inclusive measures can themselves produce new boundaries. Recognising this ambivalence is not an argument against inclusion. It is a condition for implementing it well.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Inclusion on whose terms?
Being included often means adapting to existing norms. Integration policies may expect migrants to give up parts of their identity. Labour market programmes may define participation exclusively as paid work and devalue care work or voluntary engagement. Those who do not fit the norm remain at the margin, now as “failures of integration”. Inclusion on unequal terms can thus stabilise hierarchies.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
The dilemma of difference
To receive support, people often have to be classified: as having special educational needs, as disabled, as refugees, as “at risk”. The classification opens access to resources. At the same time, it can stigmatise and separate. Martha Minow called this the dilemma of difference: ignoring difference can perpetuate disadvantage, but highlighting difference can do so as well. In German-speaking debates, the term Etikettierungs-Ressourcen-Dilemma (labelling–resources dilemma) describes the same tension in schools.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Differential inclusion
Many people are neither fully included nor fully excluded. Migration research speaks of differential inclusion: migrants are included in the labour market, for example, but with fewer rights, in insecure positions and under constant threat of exclusion. Their inclusion is real, but it is subordinate. The boundary does not run between inside and outside. It runs through the inside.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Inclusion that excludes others
Inclusion of one group can also come at the expense of another. Welfare states that strengthen solidarity among citizens may tighten access for non-citizens. Communities that grow closer may draw sharper boundaries against outsiders. Social cohesion can turn into closure.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Consequences
These ambivalences call for a critical but not cynical stance. The question is not whether inclusion is good, but how it is designed: who defines its terms, who participates in decisions, and which new boundaries emerge.
For social work practice, this means reflecting on one’s own categories and procedures. Professionals should ask regularly: whom do our offers reach, whom do they miss, and which labels do we attach to people in order to help them?






NoteReflection question



Find an example of an inclusive measure that has unintended exclusionary effects. How could the measure be redesigned?

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text: Exclusion can result from the actions of individuals, from the rules and routines of institutions and from the structures of a society. These three levels are analytically distinct. In practice they overlap and reinforce each other.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
The individual level
At the individual level, exclusion occurs in interactions: a landlord who does not rent to people with a certain name, a teacher who has lower expectations of some pupils, a remark in a meeting that marks a colleague as “other”. Prejudice, stereotypes and stigma shape such interactions. They are important, but they explain only part of the picture.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
The institutional level
Institutions can exclude even if no individual intends to do so. Mechtild Gomolla and Frank-Olaf Radtke showed for German schools that decisions about school entry, special education referrals and secondary school recommendations systematically disadvantage children with a migration background. The reason lies not primarily in individual prejudice, but in organisational routines, criteria and the pressure to produce manageable groups.
Typical mechanisms of institutional exclusion are:

formal requirements that some groups cannot meet, such as documents, language levels or fixed addresses
eligibility rules that tie access to residence status or previous contributions
standard procedures that ignore different needs
the use of categories that become labels
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
The structural level
Structural exclusion refers to the distribution of resources and power in society as a whole: in the labour market, the housing market, the education system and the political system. Charles Tilly described how durable inequality arises when categorical differences, such as citizen/non-citizen or man/woman, are linked to unequal access to resources. Exclusion is then reproduced across generations without anyone having to act intentionally.
Racism, sexism and ableism are not only attitudes. They are also inscribed in laws, institutions and social structures.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
How the levels interact
The three levels interact. Structural conditions shape institutional rules. Institutional rules give individual prejudices room to operate. Individual actions in turn confirm and stabilise structures. A housing market with little affordable housing creates competition; landlords can choose; discrimination becomes easier and harder to prove.
For social work practice, this means that individual support is necessary but not sufficient. Professionals also need to address institutional routines and, where possible, structural conditions, for example through advocacy, networking and political participation.






NoteReflection question



Choose an organisation you know, such as a school, an agency or an association. Which rules or routines could exclude certain groups, even if no one intends to do so?

title: 1.4 Key terms and conceptual distinctions
text:
Exclusion, segregation, integration and inclusion


Social exclusion

Social exclusion describes a process in which people are cut off from rights, resources and participation in the mainstream life of a society. It is multidimensional: disadvantages in income, work, housing, health, education and social contacts tend to reinforce each other. The term directs attention to the institutions and mechanisms that exclude, not only to the situation of those affected.

Often confused with: poverty. Poverty usually refers to a lack of income at a given point in time, whereas social exclusion is a process that spans several areas of life.




Segregation

Segregation means that groups are separated physically or institutionally into distinct spaces, schools or services. Those affected are inside the system, for example they attend school, but in separate institutions. Segregation can be required by law or emerge from housing markets, school choice and administrative practice.

Often confused with: exclusion. Segregated groups are not cut off from a system; they are kept apart within it.




Integration

Integration refers to incorporating individuals or groups into existing structures, such as mainstream schools or the labour market. The structures themselves largely remain unchanged, and those who are integrated are expected to adapt. In migration debates, the term covers very different meanings, ranging from equal participation to cultural adaptation.

Often confused with: inclusion, or blurred with assimilation, the demand to give up one’s own cultural identity.




Inclusion

Inclusion means changing structures so that everyone can participate fully and on equal terms. The system adapts to the diversity of people, not the other way round. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) establishes inclusive education as a right.

Often confused with: integration. Placing someone in a mainstream setting is not yet inclusion if teaching, rules and materials stay the same.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.4 Key terms and conceptual distinctions
text:
Mechanisms of exclusion


Marginalisation

Marginalisation describes how groups are pushed to the edges of power, resources and participation while formally remaining members of society. Marginalised groups have rights on paper but little influence on the decisions that affect them. The term captures positions between full participation and exclusion.

Often confused with: full exclusion, or with minority status, which refers to numbers rather than to power.




Social closure

Social closure describes how groups monopolise opportunities such as jobs, positions or membership by restricting access to insiders. The criteria for access can be credentials, origin, language or citizenship. The concept goes back to Max Weber and shows that exclusion often results from others securing their own advantages.

Often confused with: spatial separation. Social closure concerns access to resources and positions, not where people live.




Othering

Othering is the process of constructing a group as fundamentally different from and inferior to one’s own. By defining “the others”, a group stabilises its own identity as “us”. Othering takes place in language, media, policies and everyday practices.

Often confused with: individual prejudice. Othering is a collective, discursive process, not merely a personal attitude.




Stigma

A stigma is an attribute or label that discredits a person and spoils their social identity. Once stigmatised, a person is no longer seen as a whole person but is reduced to that one feature. Stigma can lead to discrimination, and it also affects how people see themselves.

Often confused with: stereotype, a cognitive generalisation about a group, or with discrimination, the unequal treatment that may follow from stigma.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.4 Key terms and conceptual distinctions
text:
Analytical and normative concepts


Intersectionality

Intersectionality analyses how categories such as race, gender, class or disability overlap and together produce specific forms of disadvantage. A Black woman, for example, may face discrimination that neither Black men nor white women experience in the same way. The term was coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in legal studies.

Often confused with: an additive model in which several forms of discrimination are simply added up.




Recognition

Recognition means being affirmed as an equal and valued member of a community. It includes legal respect as a bearer of rights and social esteem for one’s abilities and way of life. Denied recognition is experienced as an injustice in its own right.

Often confused with: tolerance, which merely puts up with difference, or with redistribution, the material side of justice.




Citizenship

Citizenship is formal membership in a political community that grants rights and duties and allows claims on the state. Who holds citizenship and who is denied it is a central line of inclusion and exclusion. Formal citizenship does not guarantee that people are treated as full members in practice.

Often confused with: nationality, or with substantive belonging, which can be missing despite a passport.




Reasonable accommodation

Reasonable accommodation means necessary and appropriate adjustments in an individual case that enable a disabled person to exercise their rights on an equal basis with others. Examples are extra time in exams or an adapted workplace. Under the CRPD, denying reasonable accommodation counts as discrimination.

Often confused with: accessibility or universal design, which apply to everyone in advance rather than responding to one person’s needs.




Capability approach

The capability approach judges well-being by people’s real freedoms to do and be what they have reason to value. It asks not only which resources people have but what they can actually achieve with them. Developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, it is widely used to assess social justice and development.

Often confused with: income or resource measures, or with skills and competencies in an educational sense.




Social cohesion

Social cohesion describes the degree of trust, shared belonging and cooperation that holds a community together across differences. Cohesive societies do not require sameness; they manage diversity and conflict without breaking apart. The term is common in European and national policy debates.

Often confused with: sameness or assimilation, or with social capital, the resources people gain from their networks.

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
text: Modern societies promise equal participation. Constitutions, human rights treaties and welfare states formulate the claim that every person should have access to education, work, health care and political participation. At the same time, inequality persists, and in some areas it grows. The tension between the promise of inclusion and the reality of exclusion is a defining feature of contemporary societies.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
section: From “above and below” to “inside and outside”
text:
From “above and below” to “inside and outside”
For a long time, social inequality was mainly described in terms of class and stratification: who is above and who is below. Since the 1980s, a second image has gained ground: who is inside and who is outside. Long-term unemployment, precarious work, the concentration of poverty in certain neighbourhoods and the exclusion of migrants from rights made it clear that some people are not simply lower in the hierarchy. They risk losing their connection to central areas of society altogether.
The two images do not replace each other. Inequality and exclusion are linked. But the language of inclusion and exclusion directs attention to thresholds, boundaries and processes of detachment.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
section: Areas where the boundaries become visible
text:
Areas where the boundaries become visible
Inclusion and exclusion matter in almost every area of life:

Education: access to schools, segregated school systems, educational qualifications as gateways
Labour market: unemployment, precarious employment, recognition of foreign qualifications
Citizenship and residence: voting rights, access to social benefits, deportation
Health and care: access to services, barriers for people without insurance or without a secure status
Housing and urban space: segregation, displacement, homelessness
Political participation and public discourse: whose voice is heard and whose is not
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
section: Inclusion as a political and normative goal
text:
Inclusion as a political and normative goal
Inclusion has also become a political programme. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities establishes inclusion as a human rights obligation. The European Union has made the fight against poverty and social exclusion a policy goal. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development commits states to “leave no one behind”.


2006 United Nations
UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
Inclusion becomes a human rights obligation.


2010 European Union
Europe 2020 strategy
A headline target: fewer people at risk of poverty or social exclusion.


2015 United Nations
2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
All states commit to “leave no one behind”.


2021 European Union
European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan
A new target for reducing poverty and social exclusion by 2030.


Such commitments are important. They create a reference point for claims and for criticism. Yet they also raise questions. Who defines what full participation means? Which forms of difference are recognised, and which are expected to disappear? These questions run through the whole seminar.






NoteReflection question



In which of the areas listed above do you see the strongest boundaries in your own country? What evidence would you need to support your assessment?

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
A young woman with a migration history finishes school with good grades but receives no invitations to job interviews. A wheelchair user can enrol at a university, but the seminar room is on the second floor of a building without a lift. A family lives in a city for twenty years without the right to vote in national elections. All three are formally part of society. Yet each of them experiences a boundary: between those who belong fully and those who belong only partly, conditionally or not at all.
These scenes condense the subject of this seminar. Inclusion and exclusion describe how societies draw and shift such boundaries. They concern access to rights, resources and recognition, and they concern the question of who defines the rules of access.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
Why the topic matters
The terms have become key words of public debate. They appear in education policy, in disability rights, in migration and integration policy, in poverty reports and in the programmes of international organisations. Their popularity has a downside. The more often they are used, the less clear their meaning becomes. “Inclusion” can mean a human right, a school reform or simply a friendly gesture. “Exclusion” can describe extreme poverty, but also a lack of contacts or a missing passport.
This seminar therefore asks for precision. It treats inclusion and exclusion not as slogans, but as analytical concepts. They help to describe social positions, to identify mechanisms and to evaluate institutions.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
Relevance for social work
Social work operates at the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion. Its addressees are often people whose participation is restricted: through poverty, disability, residence status, racism or age. At the same time, social work is itself part of the institutions that grant or deny access. It decides about eligibility, assigns support and categorises cases.
For professional practice, this means a double task. Social workers support people in gaining access. And they reflect critically on how their own organisations include and exclude.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
Why an international perspective?
Comparing countries shows that the same terms describe very different practices. A school system that calls itself inclusive in one country may still separate children in another sense. Citizenship rules, welfare regimes and anti-discrimination laws vary widely. The comparison sharpens the view of one’s own society. What appears natural at home turns out to be one option among several.






NoteReflection question



Think of a situation from your everyday life or a placement in which a person was formally included but did not really belong. What made the difference?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text: The terms inclusion and exclusion are relatively young in public debate. The phenomena they describe are old. Every society has drawn boundaries between members and strangers, between the “deserving” and the “undeserving” poor, between those with rights and those without.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
Early roots in sociology
Classical sociology already dealt with belonging and its limits. Max Weber described social closure: groups secure advantages by restricting access to insiders. Georg Simmel analysed the figure of the stranger, who is part of a group and yet remains outside. Norbert Elias and John Scotson showed in their study The Established and the Outsiders (1965) how an established group stigmatises newcomers, although the two groups hardly differ socially.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
Exclusion in French social policy
The modern career of the term “exclusion” began in France. In 1974, René Lenoir published Les exclus, a book about people who had fallen through the net of social protection, among them people with disabilities, older people and young people without work. In the 1980s and 1990s, the term spread in French debates on long-term unemployment and the crisis of the suburbs. Robert Castel spoke of désaffiliation: the gradual loss of ties to work and social networks.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
European and international policy
From the late 1980s, the European Community and later the European Union adopted the language of social exclusion. It allowed poverty to be described as more than a lack of income. Since then, EU indicators have measured the risk of “poverty or social exclusion”. International organisations took up the concept as well.
In parallel, sociologists developed different readings of exclusion. Hilary Silver (1994) distinguished three paradigms: exclusion as a breakdown of social solidarity, as a result of specialisation and individual choice, and as an outcome of group monopolies. Ruth Levitas (1998) showed that political discourses use the term in different ways: to argue for redistribution, to emphasise integration into paid work, or to blame an allegedly deviant “underclass”.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
section: Inclusion in education and disability rights
text:
Inclusion in education and disability rights
The term inclusion has a second, partly separate origin in education and the disability rights movement. The UNESCO Salamanca Statement (1994) called for schools that welcome all children. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) made inclusion a binding human right. Here, inclusion stands for a change of systems rather than for the adaptation of individuals.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
Systems theory
In German-speaking sociology, Niklas Luhmann used inclusion and exclusion in a different sense. For him, inclusion means that persons are taken into account by function systems such as the economy, law or education. Exclusion in one system can trigger exclusion in others.
The concepts thus have several histories. Knowing these histories helps to understand why the same words carry different meanings today.






NoteReflection question



Compare the French debate on exclusion with the disability rights debate on inclusion. What problem does each of them address, and what solution do they suggest?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text: Inclusion and exclusion are not characteristics of individuals. Nobody is “excluded” in the way they are tall or short. The terms describe relations: between people and groups, between people and institutions, and between those who draw boundaries and those who are affected by them.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text:
No inside without an outside
Every inclusion implies a boundary. A community, a nation or an organisation defines who belongs. In doing so, it also defines who does not belong. Citizenship is a clear example. It grants rights to members and, at the same time, distinguishes them from non-citizens. Inclusion and exclusion are therefore two sides of the same process, not opposites that exclude each other.
This has an important consequence. Whoever asks why some people are excluded must also ask who includes, on what terms and in whose interest.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text:
Boundaries are made
The established–outsider study by Norbert Elias and John Scotson illustrates this. In an English suburb, an older group of residents looked down on newcomers, although both groups had similar jobs and incomes. The only difference was the length of residence. The established group used gossip, cohesion and control over local institutions to keep the newcomers in an inferior position. The boundary did not result from differences between the groups. It produced them.
Similar processes can be observed today: in debates on “real” members of a nation, in the distinction between “us” and “migrants” in the third generation, or in neighbourhoods that are labelled as problem areas.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
section: Inclusion depends on the reference point
text:
Inclusion depends on the reference point
Whether someone counts as included depends on the reference point. A person can be well integrated into family and community networks but excluded from the labour market. A refugee can attend a language course but have no right to work. A pupil can attend a mainstream school but sit in a separate group most of the day. One should therefore always ask: included in what, and excluded from what?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text:
Consequences for analysis and practice
A relational view avoids two shortcuts. The first locates the causes of exclusion solely in the deficits of individuals. The second treats people as passive victims of structures. Both overlook that boundaries are negotiated and contested, and that people respond to them.
For social work practice, this means: look at the relations, not only at the “case”. Ask who holds the power to define boundaries and what scope for action the people concerned have.






NoteReflection question



Choose a group that is often described as “excluded”. Who draws the boundary in this case, and which institutions are involved?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text: Exclusion is rarely a single event. It usually develops over time and across several areas of life. Inclusion, too, is not a state that is achieved once and for all. Both are processes.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Exclusion as a process
Robert Castel described exclusion as a gradual movement from a zone of integration through a zone of vulnerability into a zone of désaffiliation. A person loses a stable job, takes up precarious work, falls into debt, loses the flat, and contacts thin out. Each step makes the next one more likely. Seen this way, exclusion is not a fixed position at the margin, but the result of a trajectory.
This perspective has practical value. It shows that there are points at which a downward process can be interrupted, and that prevention is possible.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Multiple dimensions
Exclusion has several dimensions that reinforce each other:

economic: income, work, housing
social: networks, contacts, support
political and legal: rights, residence status, participation
cultural and symbolic: recognition, stigma, representation

A person can be included in one dimension and excluded in another. Problems tend to accumulate, however. Poverty restricts social contacts; an insecure residence status blocks access to work; stigma makes it harder to claim rights. Research therefore speaks of cumulative disadvantage.

1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Intersectionality
Dimensions of difference also overlap. Gender, race, class, disability, age and residence status do not simply add up. They interact and produce specific positions. An older woman with a refugee background experiences different barriers than a young man with the same background. Intersectional analysis helps to recognise such positions and to avoid one-dimensional explanations.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Inclusion is never finished
Inclusion processes can be reversed. Rights that were granted can be restricted. Reforms can be implemented half-heartedly. Groups that were once accepted can become targets of new exclusion, for example in times of crisis or political polarisation. Inclusion therefore requires constant attention and is always contested.
For social work practice, this means that biographies and life courses matter. Professionals need to understand how disadvantages have built up over time, and where there are points for intervention.






NoteReflection question



Describe a possible path into exclusion for a fictional person. At which points could social work have intervened?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text: Talking about inclusion and exclusion is never purely descriptive. Whoever calls a situation “exclusion” implies that something is wrong. The debate therefore rests on normative foundations. Four of them are central: equality, freedom, justice and human dignity.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Human dignity
Human dignity is the starting point. Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. The German Basic Law opens with the principle that human dignity shall be inviolable. Dignity does not depend on achievement, origin or usefulness. It is the reason why exclusion from basic rights cannot be justified by such criteria.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Equality
Equality has several meanings. Formal equality means equal rights and equal treatment before the law. Substantive equality asks whether people actually have equal opportunities. Equal treatment can produce unequal outcomes if starting conditions differ. This is why the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires reasonable accommodation, and why anti-discrimination law also covers indirect discrimination.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Freedom
Freedom is often understood negatively, as protection from interference. Exclusion, however, also restricts freedom in a positive sense: the real possibility to shape one’s own life. Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed the capability approach to capture this. What counts is not only which resources people have, but what they can actually do and be with them.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Justice
Theories of justice offer different answers to the question of what a just society owes its members. John Rawls focused on the fair distribution of basic goods. Nancy Fraser argued that justice requires redistribution, recognition and representation, so that everyone can participate as a peer in social life. Axel Honneth emphasised that misrecognition, such as disrespect and humiliation, is an injustice in its own right.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Tensions between the principles
The principles do not always point in the same direction. Equal treatment can conflict with the recognition of difference. Freedom of association can conflict with non-discrimination. Such tensions cannot be resolved once and for all. They must be weighed in each context.

1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
section: Social work as a human rights profession
text:
Social work as a human rights profession
The global definition of social work by the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) names social justice, human rights, collective responsibility and respect for diversities as central principles. For social work practice, this means that the normative foundations are not abstract. They are a professional mandate: to make exclusion visible, to justify interventions and to take a position where rights are violated.






NoteReflection question



Take a concrete case of exclusion. Which principle (equality, freedom, justice, dignity) is violated most clearly, and why?
