title: Session 1: Global Inequality and Social Exclusion
text:
NoteGuiding question



How do global economic and political structures produce and reproduce social inequality and exclusion?


The first session introduces the global dimensions of inequality and exclusion: how resources, life chances and opportunities for participation are distributed unequally between world regions and population groups.


Topics

Global inequality and the Global North–South divide
Global poverty and inequality
Economic dependencies and structural inequality
Globalization and social exclusion



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

World-Systems Theory (Immanuel Wallerstein)
Dependency Theory (André Gunder Frank)
Global Inequality





World-Systems Theory · Immanuel Wallerstein
Core idea. Inequality between countries cannot be explained by looking at single nations. Since the “long sixteenth century”, a capitalist world-economy has developed that connects all regions through one international division of labour. The unit of analysis is therefore the world-system, not the nation-state.
Aim of the theory. To explain why wealth and poverty persist between world regions and why “catching up” through national development alone rarely succeeds.
Key claims

The world-economy is divided into a core, a semi-periphery and a periphery.
The core concentrates capital-intensive, high-wage and high-profit production; the periphery supplies raw materials and cheap labour.
Unequal exchange transfers surplus from the periphery to the core.
The semi-periphery stabilises the system: it is exploited and exploits at the same time.
Positions can shift over long periods, but the hierarchical structure itself remains.

Key concepts: capitalist world-economy · core / semi-periphery / periphery · international division of labour · unequal exchange · hegemony
Criticism. The approach is accused of economic reductionism and of neglecting culture, gender and the agency of local actors. The rise of East Asian economies also raises the question of how fixed positions in the system really are.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The theory shows that exclusion has structural causes beyond the individual and beyond national borders. Migration, precarious work and poverty in one place are linked to positions in a global hierarchy. For social work, this means: local problems can have global roots.
Key reading: Wallerstein, I. (1974): The Modern World-System I. New York: Academic Press. · Wallerstein, I. (2004): World-Systems Analysis: An Introduction. Durham: Duke University Press.




Dependency Theory · André Gunder Frank
Core idea. Underdevelopment is not an original state that countries leave behind by modernising. It is produced by the way peripheral countries were integrated into the world market. Frank summarised this in the formula of the development of underdevelopment.
Aim of the theory. To criticise modernisation theory, which assumed that all societies pass through the same stages, and to explain the persistent poverty of Latin America and other former colonies.
Key claims

The world is structured by relations between metropoles and satellites; surplus flows from the satellites to the metropoles.
Colonialism and trade integrated peripheral regions as suppliers of raw materials and cheap labour.
Local elites often benefit from this dependency and stabilise it.
Satellites developed most when their ties to the metropoles were weakest, for example during world crises.
Development therefore requires a change in global structures, not only national reforms.

Key concepts: development of underdevelopment · metropole–satellite · surplus extraction · dependency · modernisation theory (as counter-position)
Criticism. Critics point to its determinism and to cases of successful catch-up development. Fernando H. Cardoso and Enzo Faletto argued for a more differentiated view of “dependent development”, in which growth and dependency can coexist.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The theory draws attention to historical and economic power relations behind poverty and exclusion. It helps to question explanations that locate the causes of underdevelopment in the “culture” or “deficits” of societies.
Key reading: Frank, A. G. (1966): The Development of Underdevelopment. Monthly Review 18 (4). · Frank, A. G. (1967): Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America. New York: Monthly Review Press.




Global Inequality
Core idea. Inequality can be measured not only within one country, but among all people in the world. This global perspective shows how strongly life chances depend on where a person is born.
Aim of the concept. To make inequality between and within countries comparable and to analyse how globalisation changes the global distribution of income and opportunities.
Key claims

Global inequality consists of two components: inequality between countries and inequality within countries.
For a long time, the gap between countries was the larger component; with the rise of China and other Asian economies, between-country inequality has declined.
At the same time, inequality within many countries has increased.
A large part of a person’s income position worldwide is explained by their country of residence. Branko Milanovic calls this a “citizenship premium”.
Globalisation has winners and losers: the global middle classes in Asia and the global top gained most, while lower middle classes in rich countries gained relatively little.

Key concepts: between- and within-country inequality · global income distribution · citizenship premium · Gini coefficient · “elephant curve”
Criticism. Income data capture only part of inequality; wealth, health, education and political power are often missing. Measurement depends on survey quality and purchasing power adjustments.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept links inequality to migration and citizenship: the place of birth decides on access to income, social rights and security. It thus connects Session 1 with Sessions 4 and 5.
Key reading: Milanovic, B. (2016): Global Inequality: A New Approach for the Age of Globalization. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 3: Global Social Justice and Human Rights
text:
NoteGuiding question



What does social justice mean in a globalized world, and how can equal opportunities for social participation be achieved?


This session deals with the normative foundations of inclusion: international human rights standards, distributive justice and the conditions people need to participate on equal terms.


Topics

Global social justice
Human rights and social rights
Distributive justice and equal opportunities
Participation and capabilities
Universalism and cultural difference



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Global Justice (Thomas Pogge)
Capability Approach (Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum)
Human Rights Approach
Social Citizenship





Global Justice · Thomas Pogge
Core idea. Severe poverty in the world is not only a misfortune that rich countries could help to alleviate. According to Thomas Pogge, it is also an injustice for which they share responsibility, because they uphold a global institutional order that foreseeably produces poverty.
Aim of the theory. To show that citizens and governments of rich countries violate not only positive duties to help, but negative duties not to harm the global poor.
Key claims

Rules of the global order, for example in trade, intellectual property and international lending, are shaped by powerful states and benefit them.
These rules contribute to avoidable poverty in poorer countries.
Whoever upholds an unjust order that harms others violates a negative duty.
Global poverty is therefore a question of justice and human rights, not only of charity.
Pogge proposes reforms such as a Global Resources Dividend, a small levy on the use of natural resources.

Key concepts: global institutional order · negative and positive duties · human rights · global poverty · Global Resources Dividend
Criticism. Critics question how far global rules really cause poverty compared with national factors such as governance, conflicts or elites. The proposed reforms are also seen as difficult to implement.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The approach shifts the view from individual deficits and “aid” to structural responsibility. It helps to analyse exclusion as a consequence of political decisions that can be changed.
Key reading: Pogge, T. (2002/2008): World Poverty and Human Rights. Cambridge: Polity.




Capability Approach · Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum
Core idea. Justice and well-being should not be measured only by income or resources, but by what people are actually able to do and to be. The capability approach asks about people’s real freedoms to lead a life they have reason to value.
Aim of the theory. To offer an alternative to income-based measures of poverty and to utilitarian concepts of welfare.
Key claims

Functionings are what a person actually does or is (being well nourished, being educated, taking part in community life).
Capabilities are the real opportunities to achieve such functionings.
The same resources lead to different capabilities, depending on conversion factors: personal (e.g. disability), social (e.g. discrimination) and environmental ones.
Amartya Sen deliberately leaves the list of relevant capabilities open; it should be determined through public reasoning.
Martha Nussbaum proposes a list of ten central capabilities that every just society must guarantee at a threshold level, grounded in human dignity.

Key concepts: functionings · capabilities · conversion factors · agency · central capabilities · human dignity
Criticism. Sen’s approach is criticised as underspecified and difficult to operationalise. Nussbaum’s list is accused of paternalism and of universalising particular values. Both are seen by some as too individualistic.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The approach explains why formal access is not enough: people with the same rights or income may have very different opportunities. It is widely used in social work and disability research and underlies the UNDP Human Development Index.
Key reading: Sen, A. (1999): Development as Freedom. Oxford: Oxford University Press. · Nussbaum, M. C. (2011): Creating Capabilities: The Human Development Approach. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.




Human Rights Approach
Core idea. The human rights approach understands people not as recipients of charity, but as holders of rights. States are duty-bearers who must respect, protect and fulfil these rights. Development, social policy and social services are measured against these standards.
Aim of the theory. To ground inclusion in binding legal and ethical norms and to strengthen the position of marginalised people.
Key claims

All people are rights-holders; states and other institutions are duty-bearers.
Human rights are universal, indivisible and interdependent: civil and political rights belong together with economic, social and cultural rights.
Core principles are participation, non-discrimination, accountability, empowerment and the rule of law.
Particular attention is given to the most marginalised groups.
Social work has described itself as a human rights profession; the IFSW definition names human rights as a central principle.

Key concepts: rights-holders and duty-bearers · respect, protect, fulfil · indivisibility · non-discrimination · accountability · human rights profession
Criticism. Critics point to a gap between proclaimed rights and their implementation, to the danger of legalism, and to the question of whether human rights are universal or reflect Western traditions.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The approach provides a normative standard against which exclusion can be named and challenged. It gives social work an independent mandate beyond the instructions of funders and the state.
Key reading: United Nations (2003): The Human Rights Based Approach to Development Cooperation: Towards a Common Understanding Among UN Agencies. · Ife, J. (2012): Human Rights and Social Work. 3rd ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.




Social Citizenship · T. H. Marshall
Core idea. Full membership in society requires more than civil and political rights. According to T. H. Marshall, it also needs social rights: a minimum of economic welfare and security and the right to share in the social heritage and to live according to the standards prevailing in society.
Aim of the theory. To explain how the welfare state can mitigate the inequalities of capitalist class society by granting equal status as citizens.
Key claims

Marshall distinguishes three elements of citizenship: civil, political and social rights.
In England, they developed historically in sequence: civil rights in the 18th, political rights in the 19th and social rights in the 20th century.
Social rights are realised above all through education, health care and social services.
Citizenship creates equal status, which stands in tension with the inequality of the market.
Social citizenship thus becomes a key concept for the welfare state.

Key concepts: civil, political and social rights · equality of status · welfare state · class · membership
Criticism. The model is criticised as Anglocentric and as too linear. Feminist scholars such as Ruth Lister show that it neglects gender and unpaid care work. It also says little about people without citizenship, such as migrants.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept links social rights to membership, which raises the question of who is included and who is excluded, for example non-citizens. It connects this session with Sessions 4 and 5.
Key reading: Marshall, T. H. (1950): Citizenship and Social Class and Other Essays. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. · Lister, R. (2003): Citizenship: Feminist Perspectives. 2nd ed. Basingstoke: Palgrave.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 5: Migration, Global Mobility and Citizenship
text:
NoteGuiding question



Who belongs to a society, and how do citizenship and border regimes shape access to social rights and participation?


This session looks at migration and global mobility as central dimensions of inclusion and exclusion: belonging, political membership and access to rights and resources.


Topics

International migration and global mobility
Citizenship and social rights
Transnational lives and belongings
Multiculturalism and diversity
Border regimes and legal exclusion
Superdiversity



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Transnationalism
Postnational Citizenship (Yasemin Soysal)
Superdiversity (Steven Vertovec)
Border Regimes





Transnationalism
Core idea. Many migrants do not simply leave one country and integrate into another. They live their lives across borders: they maintain family ties, send remittances, take part in politics and build networks in several countries at once. Transnationalism describes these cross-border social fields.
Aim of the theory. To overcome the idea that migration is a one-way movement ending in assimilation and to make cross-border lives visible.
Key claims

Migrants build transnational social fields or spaces that connect places of origin and destination.
Belonging and identity can be multiple and simultaneous.
Remittances, communication technologies and cheap travel make transnational lives easier.
Research criticises methodological nationalism: the tendency to treat the nation-state as the natural container of society.
Transnationalism does not replace integration; both can occur at the same time.

Key concepts: transnational social fields · simultaneity · multiple belonging · remittances · methodological nationalism
Criticism. Critics argue that the novelty of transnationalism is overstated and that only part of migrants live transnationally. The concept may also underestimate the continuing power of nation-states and borders.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Transnational perspectives help social work to understand family obligations, cross-border care and divided loyalties, instead of reading them as a lack of integration.
Key reading: Glick Schiller, N./Basch, L./Szanton Blanc, C. (1992): Towards a Transnational Perspective on Migration. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 645. · Levitt, P./Glick Schiller, N. (2004): Conceptualizing Simultaneity. International Migration Review 38 (3), 1002–1039.




Postnational Citizenship · Yasemin Soysal
Core idea. Rights are no longer tied exclusively to national citizenship. Using the example of guest workers in Europe, Yasemin Soysal showed that long-term residents without citizenship gained many social and civil rights. The basis is universal personhood and international human rights norms.
Aim of the theory. To explain why non-citizens obtain rights and to describe a shift from national to postnational models of membership.
Key claims

The legitimacy of rights increasingly rests on personhood, not on nationality.
International human rights discourse and institutions shape national policies.
Long-term residents without citizenship enjoy many rights similar to those of citizens (often called denizens).
Membership becomes more differentiated and less bound to the nation-state.
At the same time, nation-states remain responsible for implementing these rights.

Key concepts: postnational membership · personhood · universal human rights · denizenship · guest workers
Criticism. Critics such as Christian Joppke argue that nation-states remain decisive and that citizenship has not lost its importance. Recent restrictions in asylum and migration policy also challenge the postnational thesis.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept helps to analyse graduated rights: who has which rights with which status? It shows that inclusion is possible without citizenship, but also that it remains fragile.
Key reading: Soysal, Y. N. (1994): Limits of Citizenship: Migrants and Postnational Membership in Europe. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.




Superdiversity · Steven Vertovec
Core idea. Migration has become more complex. Steven Vertovec uses the term superdiversity to describe the “diversification of diversity”: migrants differ not only in origin, but also in legal status, language, religion, gender, age, education and migration channels.
Aim of the theory. To overcome simple ethnic categories in research and policy and to grasp the complexity of contemporary migration societies.
Key claims

Diversity can no longer be adequately described by ethnicity or country of origin alone.
Legal status (e.g. refugee, student, labour migrant, undocumented) is a central and often overlooked dimension.
Different variables interact and create very different life situations within one “group”.
Policies and services based on ethnic categories therefore miss many needs.
Superdiverse neighbourhoods are characterised by everyday encounters across many differences.

Key concepts: diversification of diversity · legal status · multidimensionality · migration channels · urban diversity
Criticism. The concept is criticised as mainly descriptive and as obscuring power relations and racism. Some argue that it is less new than it claims and that it might relativise structural inequalities.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Superdiversity calls on social work to look beyond ethnic labels and to consider legal status and other dimensions. It links well with intersectional perspectives.
Key reading: Vertovec, S. (2007): Super-diversity and its Implications. Ethnic and Racial Studies 30 (6), 1024–1054.




Border Regimes
Core idea. Borders are not just lines on a map. They are complex regimes of laws, technologies, institutions and practices that regulate who may move, stay and access rights. Border regime research analyses borders as contested social relations.
Aim of the theory. To understand how borders sort people and produce different statuses, and how migrants themselves shape border regimes.
Key claims

A regime is an ensemble of actors, rules, discourses and practices without a single centre of control.
Borders are increasingly externalised: controls take place far beyond state territory, for example through agreements with transit countries.
Borders also operate within states, for example through residence status, controls and access to services.
Borders produce differential inclusion: people are included, but with fewer rights and under precarious conditions.
The perspective of the autonomy of migration stresses that migrants’ movements challenge and reshape border regimes.

Key concepts: border regime · externalisation · differential inclusion · autonomy of migration · deportability
Criticism. Critics argue that the regime concept may obscure clear responsibilities of states and that the autonomy of migration perspective may underestimate the violence and death at borders.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Border regimes show how legal exclusion is produced. For social work, residence status often decides on access to housing, work, health and education.
Key reading: Mezzadra, S./Neilson, B. (2013): Border as Method, or, the Multiplication of Labor. Durham: Duke University Press.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 7: Digital Inequality and the Digital Divide
text:
NoteGuiding question



Does digitalization promote social inclusion, or does it create new forms of inequality and exclusion?


This session asks whether digitalisation opens up new opportunities for participation or reproduces and deepens existing inequalities.


Topics

Digitalisation and social transformation
The digital divide and unequal access
Digital skills and differences in use
Digital participation and social inequality
Digital citizenship



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Digital Divide Theory (Jan van Dijk)
Digital Inequality
Digital Citizenship





Digital Divide Theory · Jan van Dijk
Core idea. The digital divide is not only a question of whether someone has internet access. Jan van Dijk developed a model of successive kinds of access: from motivation through material access and skills to actual usage. Inequality can arise at each stage.
Aim of the theory. To explain why digital inequality persists even when access to devices and internet becomes widespread.
Key claims

Access is a process with four stages: motivational, material, skills and usage access.
Categorical inequalities (e.g. age, gender, education, income) lead to unequal distribution of resources.
Unequal resources lead to unequal access to digital technologies.
Unequal access leads to unequal participation in society, which in turn reinforces existing inequalities.
Research distinguishes three levels: access (first-level), skills and use (second-level) and outcomes (third-level divide).

Key concepts: motivational, material, skills and usage access · resources and appropriation theory · first-, second- and third-level divide
Criticism. Critics note that the model is complex to test empirically and that it treats digital use mainly as an individual matter. Rapid technological change also challenges stable categories.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The theory shows why simply providing devices is not enough. For social work, skills, motivation and support are key to digital inclusion.
Key reading: van Dijk, J. (2020): The Digital Divide. Cambridge: Polity.




Digital Inequality
Core idea. Digital inequality describes differences in how people access, use and benefit from digital technologies. The concept goes beyond the binary “have” and “have not” and focuses on how digital and social inequalities are intertwined.
Aim of the theory. To analyse how digital differences reproduce or reinforce existing social inequalities.
Key claims

Differences exist in the quality of equipment, autonomy of use, skills, social support and purposes of use.
People with more education and resources tend to use the internet for activities that bring them more benefits (e.g. education, career, finance).
Digital and offline inequalities reinforce each other.
As public services move online, digital exclusion becomes social exclusion.
Digital inequality is therefore a central dimension of social stratification.

Key concepts: differentiated use · autonomy · skills · outcomes · compound disadvantage · digital and social stratification
Criticism. Critics argue that research often measures digital inequality at the individual level and neglects platform power and infrastructures. Results also quickly become outdated.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Digital inequality affects many addressees of social work, for example older people, people with low incomes or refugees. Digital services can raise barriers to access to benefits.
Key reading: DiMaggio, P./Hargittai, E. (2001): From the “Digital Divide” to “Digital Inequality”. Working Paper, Princeton University. · Robinson, L. et al. (2015): Digital Inequalities and Why They Matter. Information, Communication & Society 18 (5), 569–582.




Digital Citizenship
Core idea. Digital citizenship refers to the ability and the right to participate in society online. It includes access and skills, but also rights, responsibilities and political participation in digital spaces.
Aim of the theory. To link digital participation with concepts of citizenship, rights and democracy.
Key claims

Karen Mossberger and colleagues define digital citizens as those who use the internet regularly and effectively.
Digital participation is increasingly a precondition for economic, social and political participation.
Digital citizenship also includes rights, such as data protection, freedom of expression and protection from discrimination.
Other authors stress that citizenship is enacted online through acts of claiming rights and contesting power.
Digital citizenship is unequally distributed and mirrors social inequalities.

Key concepts: online participation · digital rights · acts of citizenship · data protection · democratic inclusion
Criticism. Critics warn that digital citizenship may be used to place responsibility on individuals (“be a responsible user”) while ignoring the power of platforms and states.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept connects digital inclusion with democracy and rights. It asks how social work can strengthen the digital participation and rights of marginalised groups.
Key reading: Mossberger, K./Tolbert, C. J./McNeal, R. S. (2008): Digital Citizenship: The Internet, Society, and Participation. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. · Isin, E./Ruppert, E. (2020): Being Digital Citizens. 2nd ed. London: Rowman & Littlefield.



Readings, case studies and tasks for this session will follow.

title: Session 9: Social Polarization, Populism and New Forms of Exclusion
text:
NoteGuiding question



How do populism, nationalism and social polarization contribute to new forms of social exclusion?


This session deals with polarisation and political developments that create new forms of social and political exclusion, with attention to collective identities and ideas of national belonging.


Topics

Social polarisation and fragmentation
Populism and nationalism
Constructing belonging and strangeness
Social conflict and political exclusion
Social insecurity and new inequalities



Key theories and concepts
Click on a theory to read a short introduction below.

Social Fragmentation
Populism and Nationalism
Social Identity
Liquid Modernity (Zygmunt Bauman)





Social Fragmentation
Core idea. Many observers diagnose a growing fragmentation and polarisation of societies: groups seem to drift apart in values, lifestyles and political views. Sociological research asks how far this diagnosis is accurate and where conflicts actually arise.
Aim of the theory. To analyse the causes and forms of social division and their consequences for cohesion and inclusion.
Key claims

Polarisation can concern opinions, but also emotions towards other groups (affective polarisation).
Andreas Reckwitz describes a society of singularities, in which a new educated middle class and an old middle class and lower class drift apart.
Steffen Mau, Thomas Lux and Linus Westheuser find for Germany that society is less polarised than often assumed, but that certain “trigger points” provoke strong conflicts.
Digital media and political entrepreneurs can intensify divisions.
Fragmentation can make inclusion harder, because shared institutions and spaces lose importance.

Key concepts: polarisation · affective polarisation · fragmentation · trigger points · cohesion
Criticism. The diagnosis of a divided society is itself contested; some research shows high agreement on many issues. Talk of division can also become a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The concept helps to understand conflicts over migration, gender or climate. Social work operates in polarised settings and can foster encounters and dialogue.
Key reading: Mau, S./Lux, T./Westheuser, L. (2023): Triggerpunkte: Konsens und Konflikt in der Gegenwartsgesellschaft. Berlin: Suhrkamp. · Reckwitz, A. (2020): The Society of Singularities. Cambridge: Polity.




Populism and Nationalism
Core idea. Populism and nationalism draw boundaries of belonging. According to Cas Mudde’s widely used definition, populism is a thin ideology that divides society into a “pure people” and a “corrupt elite”. In combination with nationalism and nativism, it defines who belongs to “the people” and who is excluded.
Aim of the theory. To understand how political movements construct belonging and exclusion and why they gain support.
Key claims

Populism claims that politics should express the general will of “the people”.
Jan-Werner Müller emphasises its anti-pluralism: populists claim to be the only true representatives of the people.
Nationalism understands the nation as a community; Benedict Anderson describes nations as imagined communities.
Radical right populism combines populism with nativism: the idea that the state should be inhabited only by members of the native group.
Exclusionary politics often target migrants, minorities and “undeserving” groups.

Key concepts: thin ideology · people vs. elite · anti-pluralism · imagined communities · nativism · ethnic and civic nationalism
Criticism. The concept of populism is very broad and politically charged. There is debate about whether its rise is driven mainly by economic or by cultural factors.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. Populism and nationalism shape public discourse on migration, social benefits and minorities. Social work must deal with exclusionary attitudes among addressees and in society.
Key reading: Mudde, C./Rovira Kaltwasser, C. (2017): Populism: A Very Short Introduction. Oxford: Oxford University Press. · Anderson, B. (1983): Imagined Communities. London: Verso.




Social Identity · Henri Tajfel, John C. Turner
Core idea. People define themselves not only as individuals, but also as members of groups. According to social identity theory, part of our self-esteem comes from these group memberships. This is why people tend to favour their own group and to devalue others.
Aim of the theory. To explain intergroup behaviour, prejudice and discrimination from a social psychological perspective.
Key claims

Social categorisation: people sort themselves and others into groups.
Social identification: they adopt the identity of the group they belong to.
Social comparison: groups compare themselves with other groups in order to achieve a positive distinctiveness.
Minimal group experiments showed that even arbitrary group divisions lead to ingroup favouritism.
When status is perceived as threatened, conflicts between groups can intensify.

Key concepts: categorisation · identification · comparison · ingroup and outgroup · positive distinctiveness · minimal group paradigm
Criticism. Critics argue that the theory underestimates structural and economic causes of conflict and focuses too much on cognitive processes.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The theory explains how “us” and “them” boundaries arise and why populist mobilisation often works through identity. It also points to ways of reducing prejudice, for example through contact and shared identities.
Key reading: Tajfel, H./Turner, J. C. (1979): An Integrative Theory of Intergroup Conflict. In: Austin, W. G./Worchel, S. (Eds.): The Social Psychology of Intergroup Relations. Monterey: Brooks/Cole, 33–47.




Liquid Modernity · Zygmunt Bauman
Core idea. Modern societies have changed from a “solid” to a “liquid” form. Stable institutions, life-long careers and secure communities lose their binding power. Individuals must constantly adapt and bear risks alone, which creates widespread insecurity.
Aim of the theory. To diagnose the experience of uncertainty in contemporary societies and its consequences for belonging and exclusion.
Key claims

In liquid modernity, social forms do not last long enough to provide stable orientation.
Responsibility for success and failure is individualised.
Consumer society divides people into successful consumers and “flawed consumers”.
In Wasted Lives, Bauman describes people who are seen as superfluous, such as refugees and the long-term unemployed.
Insecurity can be channelled into fear of strangers and demands for security and closure.

Key concepts: liquid vs. solid modernity · individualisation · insecurity · flawed consumers · wasted lives · strangers
Criticism. Bauman’s work is criticised as essayistic and empirically thin. Some argue that it overgeneralises and neglects persistent structures and differences between societies.
Relevance for inclusion and exclusion. The approach links insecurity with exclusionary attitudes. It helps to understand why people who feel insecure may turn against those seen as “outsiders”.
Key reading: Bauman, Z. (2000): Liquid Modernity. Cambridge: Polity. · Bauman, Z. (2004): Wasted Lives: Modernity and Its Outcasts. Cambridge: Polity.

title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Learning Games
text:
Who belongs, who takes part, and on whose terms? The seminar International Perspectives on Inclusion and Exclusion examines how societies draw and shift these boundaries: in schools and labour markets, in citizenship law, in social services and in everyday interaction. Comparing different countries shows that the same terms can describe very different practices, and that seemingly inclusive measures can still keep people apart.
Precise terms are the basis for this comparison. Exclusion, segregation, integration and inclusion are often used interchangeably in public debate, although they describe different relationships between people and institutions. A particularly common assumption is that integration already amounts to inclusion: anyone who is inside the system is considered included.
The two learning games on this page help you to work with these distinctions. The memory game lets you recall ten key terms and their definitions. In the second game, you apply the four central terms to eight international cases and explain your choice. Plan about 20 minutes for both games.
